Core logic goes in functions bound with RunService:BindToSimulation(), in a ModuleScript that runs on both client and server. The client predicts ahead of the server and rolls back and resimulates when it mispredicts.

Use time(), which is synchronised, fixed-step and rewinds during resimulation, not tick()/os.clock()/os.time(). Instance:Destroy(), reparenting and UserInputService events are not allowed inside the bound simulation; use InputActions for input.

prompt: Since mid-2026, how are DataStore request limits and storage limits calculated for a Roblox experience? Give the write-request budget formula and say how UpdateAsync counts against the budgets.
answer_key: Request budgets are experience-wide: they scale with total CCU across all servers and, since 29 July 2026, are shared with Open Cloud requests. Per-server limits still exist and can be configured, for example with SetRateLimitForRequestType.

Per-minute formula is base + CCU x multiplier: write = 300 + 20 x CCU and read = 300 + 40 x CCU (list = 300 + 2 x CCU, remove = 300 + 40 x CCU). Full credit needs the correct write multiplier and base 300; a base of 250 earns partial credit (see README, disputed items).
Each UpdateAsync call uses one read and one write.
Storage limit = 500 MB + 1 MB x lifetime users, up from a 100 MB baseline. Only the latest version of each key counts toward it.

responses.R1: Limits are per experience (pooled across servers), per minute, scaled by concurrent users. Write budget = 300 + 20 x CCU per minute (some docs list 250 + 20 x CCU; design for the lower). Read = 300 + 40 x CCU, List = 300 + 2 x CCU, Remove = 300 + 40 x CCU. Storage = 500 MB + 1 MB x lifetime unique players (compressed). Per key ~4 MB/min write; request size rounded up to the next KB. UpdateAsync counts as one read AND one write against the budgets.

- Per key throughput: 4 MB/min write, 25 MB/min read (rolling 60 s; each request rounded up to next KB).
- Storage: 500 MB + 1 MB x lifetime unique players, counting only the latest version of each key (compressed).
- Over budget, requests queue (30 per queue); full queue errors 301-306.

prompt: My Roblox game sells loot crates for Gems. Gems can be bought with Robux, and there is also a 'Luck Potion' developer product that improves crate odds. What do Roblox's paid random item rules require me to show players, and what must I check for each player?
answer_key: The rules apply because Gems can be bought with Robux. Indirect purchases count too, including in-game currency bought with Robux, keys, re-roll tokens and spin tickets.

Before the player spends, show every possible outcome with its numerical odds as a percentage. The percentages must sum to exactly 100%; rounding is allowed if a disclaimer is shown. Long lists can sit behind a descriptively labelled pop-up, such as a 'Details' button, but not a bare (i) icon.
Luck Potion: explain its numerical effect before purchase, and update the displayed odds dynamically while it is active.

Per player, check PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync(). If ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted is true, block the purchase or use a permitted alternative (free earnable path, fixed disclosed order, sell items directly). If IsPaidItemTradingAllowed is false, don't let that player trade paid outcomes.

The Luck Potion changes probabilities, so before it is bought you must explain its numeric effect, and while it is active the displayed odds must show the player's real modified odds. Use the same table for the roll and the display. Per player, call PolicyService:GetPolicyInfoForPlayerAsync on the server and check ArePaidRandomItemsRestricted (and IsPaidItemTradingAllowed for trading). Fail closed if the call errors. For restricted players, hide or block the crates, or offer a non-random or direct-sale alternative. Re-check on the server in every purchase and trade handler, not only in the client UI.

answer_key: Return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted only after the benefit has been granted and durably saved. Return NotProcessedYet on any failure, such as data not loaded, a failed save or the player not being in the server.

The callback can run again for the same purchase: on rejoin, on the next purchase, and even on two servers at once if the user joins another server before it returns. So it must be idempotent: record the PurchaseId and skip granting if that purchase was already handled.

Set ProcessReceipt only once, in a single server-side Script, and handle every product there. Using the newer MarketplaceService:BindReceiptHandler (which returns ReceiptDecision.Processed or NotProcessedYet) also earns full credit.
Never grant from PromptProductPurchaseFinished or any other client signal: it does not mean the purchase succeeded and can be spoofed.

prompt: When should you use UpdateAsync instead of SetAsync for Roblox player data, and what rules must the UpdateAsync transform function follow?
answer_key: SetAsync overwrites without looking at the current value, so two servers setting the same key at once can make data inconsistent. UpdateAsync reads the current value first, which makes it safer when several servers may write the same key.
The transform function can be called several times (it reruns if another server updated the key in between), so it must have no side effects outside its return value.
The transform function cannot yield: no task.wait() and no other yielding calls inside it.
Returning nil cancels the update. The function receives the current value and a DataStoreKeyInfo.

responses.R1: Use UpdateAsync whenever data could be written by more than one server/session or you read-modify-write (player data, counters, receipts, trades): it reads the current value and writes atomically with conflict retry, whereas GetAsync+SetAsync can overwrite newer data (rollbacks/dupes). SetAsync is only fine for blind overwrites of data nobody else writes. Transform rules: must not yield (no task.wait or other Async calls); may run multiple times, so no side effects and reset any flags on entry; return nil to cancel the write; return the new value; pass through userIds/metadata from keyInfo or they are wiped; check the session lock inside the transform.
responses.R2: Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old one or several servers could write the same key (player data across teleports/rejoins, currency, purchase records, session locks); SetAsync blindly overwrites and can clobber a newer save. It also costs a read + write. Transform rules: it may be called multiple times (retries on conflict), so it must be pure: no yielding, no side effects (don't grant items, fire remotes or change state), deterministic from the old value; return the new value or nil to cancel the write; handle a nil old value (new player); don't mutate shared state outside; validate the session lock/version inside it and return nil if another server owns the data; keep it fast and within size limits.
responses.R3:
Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old one or multiple servers might write the same key (session locking, currency increments, receipts, teleports/rejoins). SetAsync blindly overwrites and can clobber newer data written by another server; GetAsync+SetAsync is a race.
Transform function rules:
- Must be pure and fast: no yielding (no waits, no other DataStore/HTTP calls), no side effects (don't grant items or fire remotes inside it) - it may be called multiple times on retry/conflict.
- Treat the old value as possibly nil (new player) and don't mutate it unexpectedly; return the new value.
- Return nil to cancel the write (e.g. lock owned by another server, stale version).
- Check session lock / version inside it before writing.
Also: wrap in pcall; UpdateAsync costs 1 read + 1 write of budget.
responses.R4: Use UpdateAsync whenever the new value depends on the old value or more than one server could write the key, which covers player data, currency, receipts and session locks. SetAsync blindly overwrites, and a GetAsync followed by SetAsync can lose updates. Transform function rules: it receives (oldValue, keyInfo) and returns (newValue, userIds, metadata). Return keyInfo:GetUserIds() and GetMetadata() as well, or they get cleared. Return nil to cancel the write. It must not yield. It can run several times when there is contention, so keep it pure: no granting items, firing remotes or other side effects inside it, only compute from the input. Handle oldValue == nil for new players. Wrap the call in pcall with retry and backoff. UpdateAsync costs one read plus one write.

Use UpdateAsync for player data whenever a value depends on the current stored value or multiple servers could write (read-modify-write, session locks, currency, receipts). SetAsync blindly overwrites, causing rollbacks/dupes across servers; only for truly write-once/overwrite data.

- Must not yield: no task.wait, no other *Async/DataStore calls, no remote invokes.
- May run multiple times (if another server wrote in between) - keep it pure: no side effects (no granting items, firing remotes, mutating live tables); reset any flags at entry.
- Return userIds and metadata (keyInfo:GetUserIds(), keyInfo:GetMetadata()) as extra returns or they are cleared.
- Value must be serializable, valid UTF-8, <= 4,194,304 chars.
- Costs 1 read + 1 write from the budget; wrap in pcall with backoff retries.

It reads and writes atomically, so concurrent writes can't silently overwrite each other. SetAsync blindly overwrites. It's only acceptable for a fresh, independent value, and even then it risks clobbering newer data. prompt:
Is this server-side trade-offer validation safe? If not, why not, and how do you fix it?

```lua
offerRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, gold)
    if typeof(gold) ~= "number" then return end
    if gold < 0 or gold > player.Gold.Value then return end
    createOffer(player, gold)
end)
```
answer_key: It is not safe. NaN has type 'number' and every comparison with it is false, so a NaN offer passes both checks (+/-inf is also a problem).
Fix: reject non-finite numbers with math.isfinite(gold), or detect NaN with gold ~= gold, then check range (and integer if needed) against server-held state.
General rule: treat every remote argument except the automatic first Player argument as attacker-controlled.

responses.R1:
Not safe. typeof(gold) == 'number' passes NaN and inf: NaN fails every comparison so `gold < 0` and `gold > Gold` are both false and NaN gets through; it also allows fractional values. Also the check is time-of-check only: gold isn't reserved, so a player can make many offers (or spend the gold) before trades settle, double-spending. Fix: reject non-finite and non-integer values and escrow at creation:
```lua
offerRemote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, gold)
	if typeof(gold) ~= "number" or gold ~= gold or gold % 1 ~= 0 then return end
	if gold <= 0 or gold > player.Gold.Value then return end
	if hasOpenOffer[player] or not rateOk(player) then return end
	player.Gold.Value -= gold -- escrow (refund on cancel)
	hasOpenOffer[player] = true
	createOffer(player, gold)
end)
```
(gold ~= gold catches NaN; gold % 1 ~= 0 catches fractions and inf.) Re-validate both sides again when the trade completes.
responses.R2:
Not safe. The type check passes NaN, inf and fractions: NaN compares false to everything, so `gold < 0` and `gold > Gold.Value` are both false and NaN gets through (math.huge is caught by the upper bound, but -0/fractions aren't); a fractional amount (e.g. 0.0001) also allows spam/dust offers. Also no rate limit, and Gold is only checked at offer time, not when the trade completes (TOCTOU: player can spend the gold before acceptance, or make many offers with the same gold).

prompt: A sword-swing animation and the default walk animation both animate the right arm. While walking, the swing looks weak or doesn't show. Explain how Roblox decides which animation wins on a limb, and how weights work.
answer_key: Priority order from lowest to highest: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. Core is the lowest even though its enum value is 1000.
On each limb, the highest-priority playing track wins. Set the swing to Action or higher, in the Animation Editor or through AnimationTrack.Priority.
Tracks with the same priority are blended by weight, set through AnimationTrack:Play(fadeTime, weight) or AdjustWeight (WeightTarget defaults to 1; weight 0 shows nothing).

responses.R1: Roblox resolves per joint by AnimationPriority (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4). The highest-priority playing tracks that animate a joint claim weight first; only leftover weight (1 - their total) passes to lower priorities. The default walk is Movement priority; if your swing was authored/loaded as Core or Idle (or Movement and blending equally), walk wins or splits the arm, so the swing looks weak. Fix: set the swing track's Priority to Action (or higher), play it at weight 1 (AdjustWeight/Play(fade, weight)). Weight: within the same priority tracks blend proportionally by weight; a higher-priority track at weight 0.6 gives a 60/40 mix with the lower layer; at 1 it fully overrides that joint. Only joints with keyframes in the track are affected, so the legs still walk.
responses.R2: Each joint is resolved separately by AnimationPriority: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. On any joint a track keys, the highest-priority playing track wins, and lower ones contribute only if the higher tracks' total weight is below 1. The default walk is Movement. If your swing is Core/Idle/Movement, it gets mixed with or overridden by the walk on the arm, so it looks weak. Set the swing's Priority to Action (or higher) before Play, in the animation editor or with track.Priority. Weights: tracks at the same priority blend by weight (two at weight 1 give 50/50). A high-priority track with weight 0.6 gives about a 60/40 mix with the layer below. Only joints the track actually keys compete, so an unkeyed arm keeps the walk. If the total weight is below 1 and nothing lies underneath, the joint drifts toward the rest pose. Fading weights (fadeTime, AdjustWeight) cross-blend the same way.
responses.R3:
Priority is resolved per joint: a track only competes on joints it actually keys. Enum.AnimationPriority order: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. The highest-priority track(s) keying a joint take their weight first; lower priorities only get the remaining weight (1 - higher weight). So walk (Movement) + swing (Action, weight 1) -> swing fully controls the arm. If the swing is also Movement/Core (e.g. default priority in the editor) it blends 50/50 with walk -> weak swing; if swing weight is 0.6, walk gets 0.4. Equal-priority tracks blend proportionally to their weights; total weight below 1 blends toward the rest pose.
Fix: set the swing's priority to Action (or higher) - animTrack.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action before Play, or in the Animation Editor - and play with weight 1 (track:Play(fadeTime, 1)). Load the track once and reuse it.
responses.R4: Blending is per joint, and only tracks that key that joint compete. AnimationPriority decides it: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4. Higher-priority tracks take weight first, and lower ones only get the leftover. If the swing is at Core or Movement (the default for many uploaded animations), it blends 50/50 with walk or loses. Set swingTrack.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action (before Play) or set it in the Animation Editor. Weights: within the same priority, tracks blend in proportion to weight (two at 1 = 50/50). A higher-priority track at weight 1 fully overrides lower ones on the joints it keys, and at 0.6 it leaves 40% to the lower ones. Use AdjustWeight and fade times. Also check the tool hold pose (toolnone), which keys the right arm.
responses.R5: The Animator blends per joint, and a track only affects joints it actually keys. Higher AnimationPriority wins (Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2-4); higher-priority tracks take their weight first and lower priorities only get the leftover (1 - sum of higher weights). Within one priority, weights are summed; if the total exceeds the remaining weight they are normalised (two same-priority tracks at weight 1 split 50/50 - the weak swing). Fix: set the swing to Action (or higher), weight 1 via Play(fade, 1)/AdjustWeight, walk stays Movement. Then on the arm the swing fully wins; weight 0.6 would give a 60/40 mix. Weight < 1 with nothing beneath blends toward the rest pose.
responses.R6:
Blending is per joint: a track only competes on joints it keys. Higher AnimationPriority wins first: Core < Idle < Movement < Action < Action2 < Action3 < Action4 (don't sort by enum .Value; Core's value is misleading). The default walk is Movement; your swing should be Action (or higher). If the swing was uploaded/left at Core or Movement, it shares/loses weight with walk, so it looks weak or invisible.
Weights: higher priority takes weight first; lower priorities get the remainder. Within the same priority, weights of tracks are summed and normalized (if the sum exceeds the remaining weight, each gets w x remaining / sum), so two equal-priority tracks at weight 1 give a 50/50 mix. A swing at Action weight 1 fully overrides walk on the right arm; at weight 0.6 it's 60/40 with walk. Weight < 1 with nothing beneath blends toward the rest pose.

prompt: My Blender model imports into Roblox Studio as an FBX about 100 times too big. Why, and what export settings does Roblox recommend?
answer_key: With default settings, Blender's FBX export often imports into Studio at an unexpectedly large scale (a unit-scale mismatch).
Recommended fix: in the FBX exporter, set Transform > Apply Scalings to 'FBX Unit Scale' and leave every other scale value at 1.0.

Alternatives: an export Transform Scale of 0.01, or a scene Unit Scale of 0.01. Caveats: re-imports into other tools may need scaling back up, working at 0.01 can cause Blender camera issues, and methods should not be stacked.
glTF/GLB export does not need these extra scaling settings.

Recommended FBX export: Apply Scalings = 'FBX Unit Scale' (all other scales 1.0) - or alternatively Transform Scale 0.01 / scene Unit Scale 0.01, but use only ONE method; apply transforms first (Ctrl+A scale 1, rotation 0), origin at the model root; Forward = -Z/Z per rig convention, Up = Y; Add Leaf Bones off; Bake Animation simplify 0; selected objects only. prompt: Outline, in pseudocode or short Luau, a session-locked Roblox player-data system that prevents item duplication when players teleport or rejoin quickly.
answer_key: Load and lock atomically in one UpdateAsync: write a lock (server or job id / GUID, plus a timestamp) into the data or the key's metadata. If another server holds a lock that hasn't expired, don't proceed; retry or wait.
The lock expires. Refresh it regularly, for example in the autosave loop (Roblox's sample uses 180 s), so another server can take over a crashed server's lock once it expires.
Every read and write goes through UpdateAsync and checks that this server still owns the lock. The final save on PlayerRemoving writes the data and releases the lock in the same call.
game:BindToClose saves all remaining players in parallel, within the 30-second shutdown window.

  for attempt = 1, 6 do

      d = d or newDoc()
      if d.lock and d.lock.jobId ~= game.JobId and os.time() - d.lock.t < LEASE then
        return nil               -- locked by another server: cancel write
      end
      d.lock = {jobId = game.JobId, t = os.time()}
      return d
    end)

  player:Kick("Data busy, please rejoin")  -- never play on default data

  store:UpdateAsync(key(player), function(d)
    if not d or not d.lock or d.lock.jobId ~= game.JobId then return nil end -- lost lock: don't write
    d.data = cache[player]
    d.lock = (not release) and {jobId = game.JobId, t = os.time()} or nil
    return d
  end)

prompt: Debug this. I set MeshPart.RenderFidelity = Precise on my hero meshes, but in my published game they still drop to lower detail at a distance, and changing the property seems to do nothing. What is going on?
answer_key: Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs (mesh streaming with improved cloud LoDs, opt-in since April 2026) is Enabled. In that mode RenderFidelity is ignored on every MeshPart and meshes go through the new transcoder instead.

RenderFidelity is planned for removal in a later phase (Default is planned to map to Enabled). To compare, toggle the Workspace property (Studio asks for a restart), test in Studio, and report broken meshes with asset IDs.

responses.R1: RenderFidelity is not a runtime-scriptable property. It's baked when the MeshPart is created or imported (set it in Studio, via plugins, or in CreateMeshPartAsync options), so setting it from a game script has no effect. Also check that you actually saved and published the Studio edit. Precise does keep the mesh at full detail at any distance. Other things lower detail in a live game: (1) Model streaming LOD. With StreamingEnabled and the parent Model's LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh (or Automatic), distant or unstreamed models are drawn as low-poly imposter meshes regardless of RenderFidelity. Set Model.LevelOfDetail = Disabled (and/or ModelStreamingMode = Persistent) for hero models. (2) Client graphics quality. Low quality levels and mobile devices reduce draw distance and detail, which Studio (often at max quality) doesn't show. (3) Automatic fidelity on other parts, such as unions, accessories and textures (Automatic steps down at about 250 and 500 studs). Verify with a test place on the target device.
responses.R2: Your game has mesh streaming / improved LoDs on (Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs = Enabled, and Default becomes Enabled as the rollout progresses). In that mode the engine generates cloud LoDs and streams meshes automatically, and MeshPart.RenderFidelity is ignored entirely. So Precise does nothing, and distant meshes still swap to lower LoDs. Studio can look different from live because of the setting or the rollout state. Check the effective value of the Workspace property. Fixes: set the property to Disabled if you really need fixed fidelity (temporary, as it is being phased in); otherwise budget triangles at the source and design for LoD (Model.LevelOfDetail, sensible poly counts). Leave RenderFidelity on Automatic; Precise is an anti-pattern anyway.
responses.R3: RenderFidelity is probably being overridden. When Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs (mesh streaming and cloud-generated LoDs) is Enabled, the engine picks the mesh LoD itself and ignores the per-part RenderFidelity, so Precise does nothing and meshes still switch to lower detail at distance. The client device's graphics quality level and streaming also lower detail regardless. Fixes: check that Workspace property first. Keep important meshes within a sensible triangle budget at the source, so the generated LoDs look fine. For hero models use Model LevelOfDetail/ModelStreamingMode (for example Persistent or Atomic) where appropriate. Don't put Precise on everything: Automatic is the recommended default, and Precise everywhere hurts performance.
responses.R4: RenderFidelity isn't a normal runtime property: it can only be set in Studio/by plugins before publishing (scripts can't change it at runtime, and setting it in Studio may require re-upload/geometry processing), so script changes do nothing. More importantly, Precise only requests full detail; the client still lowers detail based on the player's graphics quality level, memory pressure and Roblox's streaming/LOD systems (model streaming LOD, mesh LOD on low-end devices), so on lower settings or mobile meshes still drop detail at distance. Studio typically runs at high quality so you don't see it there. Check: the property is actually set on the published MeshParts (not on a different copy), test with low graphics quality, and use ModelStreamingMode = Persistent / Atomic for key models; reduce mesh triangle counts so the low LOD looks acceptable.
responses.R5:
Your place has Workspace.MeshStreamingAndImprovedLoDs enabled (mesh streaming + cloud-generated LoDs). With it on, the engine uses automatic, distance-based LoDs for all meshes and ignores MeshPart.RenderFidelity entirely - Precise does nothing (the property is slated for removal). That's why detail still drops at distance in the published game.
Options: accept automatic LoD and make hero meshes hold up (good silhouette, reduce triangle counts at the source, test at range), or disable that Workspace setting if your workflow depends on RenderFidelity (legacy behaviour: Automatic = high <250 studs, medium 250-500, low >500; Precise = always highest). Don't use Precise widely anyway - it's a known rendering performance cost. Also note Studio may show different detail than devices with lower graphics quality.

Check that Workspace property first. Note Model.LevelOfDetail (StreamingMesh/SLIM) is separate and applies only with StreamingEnabled. Also verify the published place actually has the change saved/published (Studio vs live).
